metadata.methods_description: Each trial began with a fixation dot for a jittered ITI (600-1000 ms), followed by a first memory screen (1000 ms) showing lateral objects to be memorized (studied or novel), balanced by objects on the opposite side. After a 1400 ms interstimulus interval, a second memory screen (1000 ms) presented additional novel items above and below fixation, with probability of appearance manipulated between extra-load (80% present) and low-load (20% present) conditions. After a 400 ms interval, a probe appeared and participants reported the object's color via continuous mouse movement along a randomly rotated color wheel. Feedback on angular error was given for 400 ms, with corrective color feedback (1000 ms) for studied objects with errors greater than 40°.

citation_details.title: The Genus Aureobasidium From Sooty Mould Communities in Poland, Including A. epipinicola sp. nov. and A. insectorum , New to Europe
citation_details.author: Paweł Czachura, Marcin Piątek
citation_details.abstract: ABSTRACT The genus Aureobasidium contains numerous species inhabiting diverse habitats, including plants, where they live as saprobes, epiphytes, endophytes or pathogens. Sooty moulds are epiphytes forming multispecies communities on the surface of leaves or needles covered with exudates of some insects. On leaves and needles, they form black coatings and therefore have a negative impact on plants due to the reduction of photosynthesis and foliar gas exchange. Additionally, they decrease the visual aesthetic qualities of ornamental plants in urban environments. In temperate climates, sooty moulds were previously commonly assigned to the species Fumago vagans , which was proven to belong to two different species, Aureobasidium pullulans and Cladosporium herbarum . A. pullulans was indeed reported from sooty mould communities based on morphological features or using sequences of a single locus (ITS). In this study, 32 strains of Aureobasidium isolated from sooty mould communities covering leaves/needles of six ornamental woody plants from municipal greenery in Poland were subjected to multilocus (ITS, LSU, rpb2 , tef1 , tub2 ) phylogenetic analyses and morphological analyses in order to resolve their species assignment. Thirty strains were identified as A. pullulans but one strain belonged to an undescribed species A . epipinicola , and one strain was assigned to A . insectorum , a species recently described from China. This study confirms that A . pullulans is a constant inhabitant of sooty mould communities in temperate regions and reports that other Aureobasidium species may also be involved in this disease complex.
